units.title: Question forms
notes: Simple tenses need do, does or did + infinitive: Does Marta cycle to school? Where did you go?
With be, have (perfect tenses) and modal verbs, put the auxiliary before the subject: Are they ready? Have you finished? Can she swim?
When who or what is the subject, do not use do, does or did: Who phoned you? What happened?

items.q: ___ your brother need permission to go on the trip?
items.why: your brother = he, so does + infinitive

items.q: Where ___ you hand in your project yesterday?
items.why: yesterday, so past simple with did

items.q: ___ the teacher giving out the exam papers at the moment?
items.why: present continuous questions start with be

items.q: Who ___ the explanation out to the class this morning?
items.why: who is the subject, so no did

items.q: ___ they made a decision about the school trip yet?
items.why: made is a past participle, so present perfect

items.q: Why ___ you staying behind after class yesterday?
How long ___ the registration usually take?
What ___ in the discussion after I left?
items.why: what is the subject, so no did

items.q: ___ you figure out the answer without any help?
What time ___ (the lesson / start) every Monday?
I know you love sport. ___ (you / ever / try) out for the school team?
items.why: ever + present perfect for life experience

items.q: Who ___ (give) you that recommendation last week? Mr Hall did.
items.why: subject question, so past simple without did

items.q: Listen! Why ___ (the students / laugh) so loudly?
When ___ (your school / break up) for the summer last year?
items.why: last year, so did + subject + infinitive

items.q: How many people ___ (join) in the discussion yesterday? About ten did.
items.why: how many people is the subject, so no did

items.q: What means this expression?
items.why: present simple questions need does + infinitive

items.q: Where you did put the registration forms?
a: Where did you put the registration forms?

items.q: Did you went for the science club in the end?
a: Did you go for the science club in the end?

items.q: you / put off / why / have / your decision / again
a: Why have you put off your decision again?
items.why: question word + have + subject + past participle

items.q: does / homework / how often / give out / your teacher / at the weekend
a: How often does your teacher give out homework at the weekend?

units.title: Present tenses: simple, continuous and stative verbs
notes: Present simple for habits, routines and facts: The band plays every Friday. Water boils at 100 degrees.
Present continuous for now, temporary situations and fixed arrangements: I'm staying with my aunt this week. We're meeting Sam at six.
Stative verbs (know, like, love, want, understand, belong) are not used in the continuous: I love this song.
For something that started in the past and is still true, use the present perfect with for or since: I've known her for years.

items.q: The lead singer usually ___ the concert with the band's biggest hit.
items.why: usually shows a routine, so present simple with -s

items.q: Turn the TV down, please! I ___ to learn the words of this song.
Right now the band ___ their new album in a studio in London.
I ___ this track. Who sings it?
We ___ the lead singer after the show tonight. Dad has got backstage passes.
items.why: a fixed arrangement, so present continuous

items.q: My cousin ___ at a concert venue, so he often gets free tickets.
Their debut album has been in the charts ___ three months.
___ your sister still want to go solo?
items.why: want is stative, so present simple with does

items.q: This guitar ___ to the lead singer, so please don't touch it.
Be quiet, please! My favourite singer ___ (give) a performance on TV and I want to listen.
My sister ___ (not / like) background music in restaurants. She never has.
items.why: like is stative, negative with doesn't

items.q: I ___ (know) the drummer since primary school.
items.why: since + unfinished situation, so present perfect

items.q: Most bands ___ (release) a track online before the album comes out.
items.why: a general fact, so present simple

items.q: Why ___ (you / wear) headphones? I'm talking to you!
Marc ___ (stay) at his aunt's flat this week because his parents are away.
I am not understanding the words of this song.
a: I don't understand the words of this song.
I do not understand the words of this song.

items.q: The concert is starting at eight every Friday.
a: The concert starts at eight every Friday.
items.why: every Friday is a routine, so present simple

items.q: She play the piano in a jazz band at weekends.
a: She plays the piano in a jazz band at weekends.

items.q: the band / a new track / is / next month / releasing
a: The band is releasing a new track next month.
Next month the band is releasing a new track.
items.why: present continuous for a fixed plan

items.q: does / how often / your favourite singer / a performance / give / in Spain
a: How often does your favourite singer give a performance in Spain?

units.title: Past tenses: past simple, past continuous, past perfect and used to
notes: Past simple for finished actions: We moved here in 2019. Past continuous for an action in progress: At nine I was walking the dog.
A long action (past continuous) is often interrupted by a short one (past simple): I was having a shower when the phone rang.
Past perfect (had + past participle) for something that happened before another past action: When we arrived, the film had started.
used to + infinitive for past habits and states; the negative and question use use: I didn't use to like fish. Did you use to live here?

items.q: While I ___ my homework, my best friend called to say sorry.
items.why: action in progress, so past continuous

items.q: Last year my brother ___ out with his best friend over a video game.
items.why: finished action last year, so past simple

items.q: When we arrived, the teacher was angry because someone ___ the window.
items.why: it happened before we arrived, so past perfect

items.q: My sister ___ take after Mum, but now she looks more like Dad.
items.why: a past state that is no longer true

items.q: Did you ___ argue with your brother a lot when you were younger?
What ___ at ten o'clock last night when I phoned?
items.why: in progress at that moment, so past continuous

items.q: In the end he ___ that he had copied the essay.
items.why: one finished action, so past simple

items.q: It ___ heavily when we left the house, so we took umbrellas.
By the time I got to the party, most of my friends ___ home.
items.why: by the time + past, so past perfect

items.q: While the teacher ___ (warn) us about the exam, the fire alarm went off.
items.why: long action interrupted, so past continuous

items.q: I ___ (not / see) Lucy at school yesterday. Was she ill?
Dad ___ (suggest) a picnic last Sunday, but it rained all day.
Mia was upset because her best friend ___ (forget) her birthday the day before.
items.why: earlier than the other past action, so past perfect

items.q: My cousin and I ___ (not / use) to get on, but now we are best friends.
items.why: negative of used to is didn't use to

items.q: What ___ (you / talk) about when I came into the room?
items.why: action in progress when something happened

items.q: I was breaking my leg on a skiing trip two years ago.
a: I broke my leg on a skiing trip two years ago.
items.why: a short finished action needs the past simple

items.q: Did you used to argue with your parents?
a: Did you use to argue with your parents?

items.q: When I got home, my brother has already eaten all the pizza.
a: When I got home, my brother had already eaten all the pizza.
items.why: before another past action, so had + participle

items.q: talked / my friends / me / going / into / to the concert
a: My friends talked me into going to the concert.

items.q: was / the bell / when / still / I / rang / writing
a: I was still writing when the bell rang.
When the bell rang, I was still writing.
items.why: past continuous interrupted by past simple

units.title: Making comparisons
notes: Comparative + than, or less + adjective + than: Trains are faster than buses. This phone is less expensive than that one.
as + adjective + as for equal things; not as ... as means less: My room isn't as big as yours.
the + comparative, the + comparative for things that change together: The more you practise, the better you play.
Make a comparative stronger or weaker with far, much, a lot, a bit; use by far with superlatives: It's by far the best.

items.q: The second earthquake was ___ than the first one.
This bridge isn't as safe ___ the old one.
The more the ground shook, ___ people became.
A crack in a cup is ___ serious than a crack in a bridge.
The river was ___ deeper than we expected, so we couldn't cross it.
items.why: far, much or a lot before a comparative, never very

items.q: It was by ___ the worst storm of the year.
Today's waves are a ___ bigger than yesterday's.
items.why: a bit + comparative for a small difference

items.q: That was ___ frightening experience of my life.
items.why: superlative of a long adjective needs the most

items.q: Tom can run as ___ as his older brother.
items.why: between as and as, use the base form

items.q: The volcano is much ___ (active) now than it was last year.
This is the ___ (bad) flood the town has ever had.
The longer we waited for the bus, the ___ (cold) we got.
Plastic bottles float ___ (easily) than glass ones.
My phone screen didn't smash because it is ___ (thick) than yours.
Your village is ___ (far) from the volcano than mine, so you are safer.
The new building is more tall than the old one.
a: The new building is taller than the old one.

items.q: This storm isn't as bad than the last one.
a: This storm isn't as bad as the last one.
This storm isn't so bad as the last one.

items.q: It was the most biggest wave I had ever seen.
a: It was the biggest wave I had ever seen.

items.q: you run / the / the / you get / faster / more tired
a: The faster you run, the more tired you get.

items.q: as / isn't / the old bridge / the new one / strong / as
a: The old bridge isn't as strong as the new one.
The new one isn't as strong as the old bridge.

units.title: Relative clauses
notes: Use who or that for people, which or that for things, whose for possession, where for places and when for times: The girl who sits next to me is from Peru.
You can leave out who, which or that when it is the object: The film (that) we saw was brilliant. Never add an extra pronoun: NOT The film that we saw it.
Non-defining clauses add extra information between commas. Do not use that in them: My dad, who is a mechanic, fixed my bike.

items.q: The cyclist ___ overtook me was wearing a red helmet.
That's the pool ___ I learned to dive.
The girl ___ bike has no brakes should be more careful.
My coach, ___ has trained Olympic athletes, gave me a lot of encouragement.
items.why: between commas use who, not that

items.q: The skateboard ___ I bought last week rolls really fast.
I'll never forget the day ___ I first managed to balance on a surfboard.
The fitness centre, ___ opened in May, is next to my school.
items.why: extra information about a thing, so which

items.q: The boy ___ was chasing the ball slid on the wet grass.
The treatment ___ helped my knee most was swimming.
items.why: that for things in a defining clause

items.q: The woman ___ (relative pronoun) teaches our fitness class used to be a gymnast.
Madrid, ___ (relative pronoun) my parents met, is my favourite city.
The bridge ___ (relative pronoun) they constructed last year is already closed.
My friend Alba, ___ (relative pronoun) brother is a racing driver, taught me to steer a go-kart.
Summer is the season ___ (relative pronoun) most people gather on the beach.
The argument, ___ (relative pronoun) lasted an hour, ended in embarrassment.
items.why: between commas use which for things

items.q: The boy which won the race is my cousin.
a: The boy who won the race is my cousin.
The boy that won the race is my cousin.
items.why: who or that for people, not which

items.q: The bike that I borrowed it has no brakes.
a: The bike that I borrowed has no brakes.
The bike which I borrowed has no brakes.
The bike I borrowed has no brakes.

items.q: My dad, that is a mechanic, fixed the brakes.
a: My dad, who is a mechanic, fixed the brakes.
items.why: no that in a clause between commas

items.q: the girl / is / who / my cousin / the race / won
a: The girl who won the race is my cousin.
My cousin is the girl who won the race.

items.q: we / the pool / yesterday / where / was / swam / freezing
a: The pool where we swam yesterday was freezing.

units.title: Present perfect and past simple
notes: Present perfect (have/has + past participle) links the past to now, and the time is not given: I've lost my keys. She's phoned three times this morning.
Past simple for a finished time (yesterday, last week, in 2015, two days ago, when ...?): We ate out last night.
just, already and never go before the participle; yet goes at the end of negatives and questions; still goes before hasn't or haven't.
for + a period, since + a starting point: for two years, since 2021.

items.q: I ___ sugar out of my diet two months ago.
items.why: ago gives a finished time, so past simple

items.q: We ___ out three times this week, and it's only Thursday.
items.why: this week is not finished, so present perfect

items.q: I haven't heated up the soup ___.
items.why: yet at the end of a negative sentence

items.q: Oh no! The milk ___ off. Smell it!
items.why: a past event with a result now

items.q: My grandparents ___ on rice and beans when they were young.
items.why: when they were young is a finished time

items.q: She has been a vegetarian ___ 2021.
I've ___ finished my lunch, so I'm not hungry at all.
items.why: just means a very short time ago

items.q: When ___ you accidentally drop the cake?
items.why: when asks about a finished time, so past simple

items.q: He ___ hasn't eaten up his vegetables, and dinner started an hour ago.
My uncle ___ (open) his restaurant in 2015, and it is still popular.
I ___ (never / taste) anything as spicy as this curry in my life.
items.why: life experience up to now, so present perfect

items.q: How long ___ (you / know) your best friend? Are you in the same class?
items.why: started in the past and continues now

items.q: We ___ (not / eat) out last weekend because we were short of money.
items.why: last weekend is a finished time

items.q: The pizza is ready. Dad ___ (just / take) it out of the oven.
She ___ (live) in Italy for two years when she was a student, and then she came home.
items.why: a finished period in the past

items.q: I have seen that cooking programme last night.
a: I saw that cooking programme last night.
items.why: last night needs the past simple

items.q: Have you ever went to a Japanese restaurant?
a: Have you ever been to a Japanese restaurant?
Have you ever gone to a Japanese restaurant?
items.why: present perfect needs the past participle

items.q: We live in this flat since 2019.
a: We have lived in this flat since 2019.
We've lived in this flat since 2019.
We have been living in this flat since 2019.
We've been living in this flat since 2019.

items.q: you / have / eaten / ever / snails
has / the soup / down / cooled / already
a: The soup has already cooled down.

units.title: Ability and possibility: can, could, be able to, managed to, may, might
notes: Present ability: can or am/is/are able to. General ability in the past: could or was/were able to: My gran could speak three languages.
For success on one occasion in the past use managed to or was/were able to, NOT could: The door was stuck, but we managed to open it. (couldn't is fine.)
can has no infinitive, -ing form or participle, so use be able to: I'll be able to come. I've never been able to whistle.
may, might and could + infinitive (without to) say that something is possible: She might not like it.

items.q: My little sister ___ read before she started school.
The novel was really complex, but I ___ finish it in a week.
items.why: success on one occasion, so managed to

items.q: I've never ___ to draw stunning illustrations like yours.
items.why: present perfect needs been able to

items.q: Take a book with you. You ___ get bored on the train this afternoon.
items.why: might for a possible future event

items.q: It was so dark that we ___ see the words on the page.
items.why: past, and couldn't is followed by the infinitive

items.q: Will you ___ come to the book club next week?
items.why: after will, use be able to

items.q: The bookshop was closing, but we ___ to buy the last copy.
items.why: one successful occasion, and to follows able

items.q: She ___ not like the ending. She hates predictable plots.
I love ___ read in the garden in summer.
items.why: after love, use the -ing form of be able to

items.q: When I was six, I ___ (can / not) swim, but I learned a year later.
The door was locked, but in the end we ___ (manage) to open it with a card.
items.why: success on one occasion in the past

items.q: I'm sure that one day you ___ (be able) to meet your favourite author.
items.why: future of can is will be able to

items.q: Sorry, I ___ (not / be able) to finish the opening chapter last night. I fell asleep.
items.why: last night, so past of be able to

items.q: She ___ (not / manage) to get tickets for the play yesterday. They were sold out.
Since his operation last year, Grandad ___ (not / be able) to read small print.
items.why: since needs the present perfect of be able to

items.q: The exam was hard, but I could pass it.
a: The exam was hard, but I managed to pass it.
The exam was hard, but I was able to pass it.
items.why: one success in the past is not could

items.q: I will can help you with your book review tomorrow.
a: I will be able to help you with your book review tomorrow.
I'll be able to help you with your book review tomorrow.
I can help you with your book review tomorrow.

items.q: She managed finish the whole novel in one day.
a: She managed to finish the whole novel in one day.

items.q: be / might / suitable / this novel / for young children / not
a: This novel might not be suitable for young children.

items.q: to / were / find / the library / you / able
a: Were you able to find the library?
You were able to find the library.

units.title: Future plans: present simple, present continuous, be going to and will
notes: Present simple for timetables: The museum opens at ten tomorrow.
Present continuous for arrangements with a time or person already fixed: I'm seeing the dentist on Tuesday.
be going to for plans you have already decided: I'm going to learn to drive this summer.
will for promises, offers and decisions made now. Word order: I'll probably come. I probably won't come. I'm definitely going to come.

items.q: Our flight ___ at 6.45 tomorrow morning, so we can't stay up late.
We ___ bikes on Saturday. I booked them online yesterday.
I've decided. I ___ sign up for the trekking course this summer.
items.why: a plan already decided needs be going to

items.q: 'These bags are really heavy.' 'Don't worry, I ___ you a hand.'
items.why: an offer made now, so will

items.q: What time ___ the museum open tomorrow?
She ___ definitely going to get a tan on that beach.
I ___ probably stay over at my cousin's on Friday.
My grandparents ___ us off at the airport tomorrow. It's all arranged.
items.why: a fixed arrangement, so present continuous

items.q: Are you ___ look around the old town when you get there?
According to the timetable, the ferry ___ (arrive) in Palma at 7.30 tomorrow.
I ___ (meet) Carla at the station at six this evening. She's already bought the tickets.
We ___ (not / be going to / stop) over in Rome. We've decided it's too expensive.
I promise I ___ (not / forget) to send you a selfie from the top of the mountain.
What ___ (you / do) on Saturday night? Have you arranged anything with your friends?
My sister has bought a guidebook because she ___ (be going to / travel) around Japan next year.
items.why: an intention, so be going to

items.q: I won't probably come on the cruise.
a: I probably won't come on the cruise.

items.q: I'm going to definitely sign up for the trip.
a: I'm definitely going to sign up for the trip.
I am definitely going to sign up for the trip.

items.q: What time does the plane lands tomorrow?
a: What time does the plane land tomorrow?

items.q: are / in August / where / going / you / to stay
a: Where are you going to stay in August?
items.why: question word + be + subject + going to

items.q: is / my aunt / around / us / taking / on Sunday / the city
a: My aunt is taking us around the city on Sunday.
On Sunday my aunt is taking us around the city.

units.title: Future predictions: be going to, will, may/might and future continuous
notes: be going to for predictions based on something you can see or know now: Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.
will for predictions based on opinion, often with I think, I'm sure, probably: I think Brazil will win.
may, might and could + infinitive when you are less sure: Prices might go up.
Future continuous (will be + -ing) for an action in progress at a future time: This time next week I'll be lying on a beach.

items.q: Look at the queue at the cashpoint! We ___ be late for the film.
items.why: prediction from evidence you can see

items.q: I think my sister ___ financially independent before she is twenty-five.
items.why: I think + will for an opinion

items.q: This time tomorrow I ___ for bargains in the sales.
items.why: in progress at a future time, so will be + -ing

items.q: Prices ___ go up next year, but nobody really knows.
items.why: might + infinitive when you are not sure

items.q: He has spent all his allowance already. He ___ short of cash by Friday.
items.why: prediction from what we know now

items.q: I'm sure you ___ your PIN. It's your birthday!
Don't phone me at six. I ___ dinner with my grandparents then.
items.why: action in progress at six, so future continuous

items.q: Careful! That glass ___ fall off the table!
items.why: you can see it, so be going to + infinitive

items.q: Do you think people ___ cash in fifty years' time?
items.why: Do you think + will for an opinion

items.q: At nine o'clock tonight we ___ (watch) the final, so please don't call.
items.why: in progress at nine, so future continuous

items.q: He never checks his balance. One day he ___ (be going to / have) a nasty surprise.
I'm sure she ___ (will / pay) off all the money she owes by next year.
Look at those dark clouds! It ___ (be going to / rain) any minute.
items.why: you can see the clouds, so be going to

items.q: This time next week, I ___ (lie) on a beach in Menorca.
items.why: this time next week needs the future continuous

items.q: Take some extra cash. The tickets ___ (might / cost) more than you expect.
At six o'clock I will be work in the shop.
a: At six o'clock I will be working in the shop.
At six o'clock I'll be working in the shop.

items.q: I think it will rains tomorrow.
a: I think it will rain tomorrow.
items.why: after will, no -s on the verb

items.q: She might to take out some money later.
a: She might take out some money later.

items.q: will / pay off / I'm sure / he / soon / the money
a: I'm sure he will pay off the money soon.
I'm sure he will soon pay off the money.

items.q: be / you / using / will / tonight / your debit card
a: Will you be using your debit card tonight?
You will be using your debit card tonight.

units.title: The passive
notes: Form: the right tense of be + past participle: Coffee is grown in Brazil. The bridge was built in 1900. The hall is being cleaned. My bike has been stolen.
After will and modal verbs use be + past participle: It will be finished tomorrow. It must be done.
Use the passive when we don't know or don't care who does the action. Add by + agent only if it is important: This song was written by a teenager.

items.q: The plants ___ every morning by my little brother.
items.why: plural subject, so are + past participle

items.q: The kitchen floor ___ yesterday, so please take your shoes off.
Be careful! The tables ___ at the moment.
items.why: happening now, so are being + participle

items.q: The dishwasher has already ___.
items.why: present perfect passive is has been + participle

items.q: All the clothes must ___ before you go out.
This washing machine was fixed ___ my uncle.
items.why: by + the person who did it

items.q: We ___ to use our phones in class.
items.why: be allowed to is a passive form

items.q: The rubbish ___ tomorrow morning.
When ___ the recycling sorted in your town?
The dishes ___ (wash) up by my sister every evening.
items.why: every evening, so present simple passive

items.q: My bedroom ___ (paint) last summer, and it still looks new.
items.why: last summer, so past simple passive

items.q: Your bike ___ (fix) right now, so you can't use it yet.
items.why: right now, so present continuous passive

items.q: The toys ___ (not / put) away yet. They're still all over the floor.
Dinner ___ (will / serve) at eight o'clock tomorrow evening.
This mess has to ___ (clear) up before Mum gets home.
This table was make by my grandfather.
a: This table was made by my grandfather.

items.q: The windows are cleaned for a company every month.
a: The windows are cleaned by a company every month.

items.q: The floors has been swept already.
a: The floors have been swept already.

items.q: were / by / the clothes / my dad / folded
a: The clothes were folded by my dad.

items.q: be / the plants / watered / should / twice a week
a: The plants should be watered twice a week.
Should the plants be watered twice a week?

units.title: Present perfect continuous
notes: Form: have/has been + -ing: I've been waiting. She hasn't been sleeping well. Have you been crying?
Use it for an activity that started in the past and is still going on or has just stopped, often with a result you can see: You're all wet! I've been washing the car.
Use it with for, since and how long to stress how long: We've been playing for two hours.
Use the present perfect simple for finished results, for how many, and with stative verbs (know, have, like): I've had this phone for a year.

items.q: Your eyes look tired. ___ you been playing on the console all afternoon?
We've been waiting for the new smartwatch ___ January.
I ___ three portable chargers this year. They are so unreliable!
items.why: a number of finished actions, so the simple form

items.q: She ___ this fitness tracker for two weeks and she still loves it.
items.why: for + activity that continues up to now

items.q: How long ___ your brother been designing video games?
items.why: your brother = he, so has been

items.q: My hands are dirty because I've been ___ my drone.
I ___ this smart speaker since my birthday.
items.why: have for possession is a stative verb

items.q: It ___ all morning, so we haven't been able to fly the drone.
He hasn't ___ well lately because he uses his phone in bed.
I ___ (try) to fix this faulty headset for an hour, and it still doesn't work.
items.why: for an hour and not finished

items.q: How long ___ (you / use) wireless headphones? Since last year?
items.why: how long + activity up to now

items.q: She's out of breath because she ___ (run) with her new fitness tracker.
items.why: a recent activity with a visible result

items.q: They ___ (not / work) on the driverless car project for very long, only a month.
Oh no! I ___ (break) my smartwatch. Look at the screen!
items.why: one finished action with a result, so simple

items.q: We ___ (know) about the problem with the interactive whiteboard for weeks.
items.why: know is stative, so no continuous

items.q: I have been knowing him for five years.
a: I have known him for five years.
I've known him for five years.
items.why: know is not used in the continuous

items.q: She has been study robotics since September.
a: She has been studying robotics since September.
She's been studying robotics since September.

items.q: We are waiting here for two hours.
a: We have been waiting here for two hours.
We've been waiting here for two hours.
items.why: for + time up to now needs the present perfect

items.q: been / how long / you / learning / have / to code
a: How long have you been learning to code?

items.q: has / my dad / a smart speaker / been / all morning / talking to
a: My dad has been talking to a smart speaker all morning.
All morning my dad has been talking to a smart speaker.

units.title: Zero and first conditionals
notes: Zero conditional: if/when + present, present, for things that are always true: If you heat ice, it melts.
First conditional: if + present, will + infinitive, for a real future possibility: If it rains, we'll stay in. Use might when the result is not certain.
Never use will in the if-clause: If I see her (NOT will see), I'll tell her.
unless means if not: We'll be late unless we hurry. Use when for something that is sure to happen.

items.q: If you mix blue and yellow, you ___ green.
If my brother is bad-tempered tomorrow morning, I ___ him alone.
items.why: a real future situation, so will

items.q: If she ___ her qualification in June, she'll apply for the job.
items.why: present simple after if, and she takes -s

items.q: You won't make friends ___ you are more patient with people.
I'm always home by six. ___ I get in this evening, I'll call you.
People usually like you if you ___ generous and easy-going.
If we're lucky, we ___ see a famous actor, but I'm not sure.
What will you do if he ___ unreliable again?
If you don't water plants, they ___.
If Leo ___ (not / be) more organised, he'll miss the deadline next week.
My mum always gets impatient if I ___ (take) too long in the bathroom.
If it rains on Saturday, we ___ (not / go) to the beach.
Unless you ___ (say) sorry, she won't speak to you again.
What ___ (you / do) if your friend forgets your birthday next week?
When you heat water to 100 degrees, it ___ (boil).
items.why: a scientific fact, so present simple

items.q: If I will see her, I'll tell her the news.
a: If I see her, I'll tell her the news.
If I see her, I will tell her the news.

items.q: Unless you don't hurry, we'll be late.
a: Unless you hurry, we'll be late.
If you don't hurry, we'll be late.
Unless you hurry, we will be late.
If you don't hurry, we will be late.

items.q: If he is mean to you again, I talk to him.
a: If he is mean to you again, I'll talk to him.
If he is mean to you again, I will talk to him.

items.q: I'll help you / if / you ask / me / nicely
a: I'll help you if you ask me nicely.
If you ask me nicely, I'll help you.

items.q: unless / pass / she / won't / harder / she / studies
a: She won't pass unless she studies harder.
Unless she studies harder, she won't pass.

units.title: Reported statements
notes: After said or told, the tense usually moves one step back: 'I'm tired.' She said she was tired. 'I lost it.' He said he had lost it.
will becomes would, can becomes could, may becomes might, must becomes had to, am going to becomes was going to.
say something, but tell somebody something: She said (that) she was busy. She told me (that) she was busy.
Time words change too: today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day, yesterday becomes the day before.

items.q: 'I'm tired,' said Eva. Eva said she ___ tired.
items.why: present becomes past, and she takes was

items.q: He ___ me that the rumour wasn't true.
'I'll give you an update tomorrow,' she said. She said she ___ give me an update the next day.
'We saw the statement yesterday,' they said. A week later I told Dad they had seen the statement ___.
'I can't confirm it,' the manager said. The manager said he ___ confirm it.
'I've never lied to you,' he said. He claimed that he ___ lied to me.
She ___ that she had made a mistake.
items.why: told and reminded need a person after them

items.q: 'You must hand it in today,' said Mr Lee. Mr Lee said we ___ hand it in that day.
'I'm going to reveal the winner,' she said. She said she ___ going to reveal the winner.
items.why: am going to becomes was going to

items.q: 'I don't believe the rumour,' said Tom. Tom said he ___ (not / believe) the rumour.
'We are waiting for a response,' they said. They said they ___ (wait) for a response.
'I lost my phone,' said Ana. Ana said she ___ (lose) her phone.
'My prediction will come true,' he said. He said his prediction ___ (come) true.
'I may be late,' said Julia. Julia said she ___ (may / be) late.
'I've already told you,' said Dad. Dad reminded me that he ___ (already / tell) me.
She said me that she was busy.
a: She told me that she was busy.
She said that she was busy.
She said to me that she was busy.

items.q: He said that he will call me the next day.
a: He said that he would call me the next day.

items.q: He told me that he has finished the report the day before.
a: He told me that he had finished the report the day before.

items.q: told / she / me / that / was moving / her family / to Bilbao
a: She told me that her family was moving to Bilbao.

items.q: said / the teacher / would / that / the exam / be / easy
a: The teacher said that the exam would be easy.

units.title: Reported questions and reported requests
notes: In reported questions the word order is like a statement and there is no do, does or did: 'Where do you live?' He asked where I lived.
For yes/no questions use if or whether: 'Are you OK?' She asked if I was OK.
Tenses, pronouns and time words change as in reported statements: 'Why did you leave?' She asked why I had left.
Requests and orders: ask or tell + person + (not) to + infinitive: She asked me to wait. He told us not to run.

items.q: 'Where does it hurt?' The doctor asked me where ___.
items.why: statement word order and no did

items.q: 'Did you trip over the cable?' She asked me ___ I had tripped over the cable.
items.why: yes/no questions use if or whether

items.q: 'Please give me a hand.' He asked me ___ him a hand.
'Don't swallow the chewing gum!' Mum told my brother ___ the chewing gum.
items.why: negative orders use not to + infinitive

items.q: 'Have you ever passed out?' The nurse asked whether I ___ ever passed out.
'Why are you laughing?' He asked us why ___.
items.why: subject before verb in reported questions

items.q: 'Can you walk?' The coach asked me if I ___ walk.
'Will you make a promise?' She asked if I ___ make a promise.
'How did you cut yourself?' Dad wanted to know how I ___ myself.
items.why: past simple becomes past perfect, no did

items.q: 'What time is it?' A woman asked me what time ___ (it / be).
items.why: subject before verb, present becomes past

items.q: 'Do you need a plaster?' The waiter asked if I ___ (need) a plaster.
items.why: no do, and present becomes past

items.q: 'Sit down and rest your ankle.' The nurse told me ___ (sit) down and rest my ankle.
'Please don't make fun of him.' The teacher asked us ___ (not / make) fun of him.
'Where did you slip?' My mum asked me where ___ (I / slip).
'Are you giving a talk tomorrow?' He asked me whether I ___ (give) a talk the next day.
She asked me where was the first-aid box.
a: She asked me where the first-aid box was.
items.why: subject before verb in reported questions

items.q: The doctor said me to stay in bed.
a: The doctor told me to stay in bed.

items.q: The teacher asked us that we had had a quarrel.
a: The teacher asked us if we had had a quarrel.
The teacher asked us whether we had had a quarrel.
items.why: reported yes/no questions use if or whether

items.q: asked / I / had / the doctor / how / my ankle / twisted
a: The doctor asked how I had twisted my ankle.

items.q: her / told / the dog / to / not / touch / I
a: I told her not to touch the dog.

units.title: have/get something done; get someone to do something
notes: have/get + object + past participle means another person does the job for you: I had my watch repaired. She's getting her nails done.
get is more informal than have; both can be used in any tense: We're going to have the kitchen painted.
get + person + to + infinitive means you ask or persuade someone to do something: I got my brother to help me.
Add by + person only if it matters who did it: I had my portrait painted by a street artist.

items.q: I ___ my hair cut at the new salon yesterday.
She's getting her nails ___ for the wedding.
We got the waiter ___ a photo of us.
I keep blinking and rubbing my eyes. I should have them ___.
Where do you ___ your bike repaired?
He had his portrait painted ___ a street artist.
items.why: by + the person who did it

items.q: My parents are ___ a new shower fitted this week.
items.why: have something done in the continuous

items.q: I couldn't fix the laptop myself, so I got my cousin ___ at it.
Did you cut your hair yourself or did you ___?
items.why: the object goes between have and the participle

items.q: My grandmother has her shopping ___ (deliver) every Friday.
We ___ (have) our car washed last Saturday because it was filthy.
items.why: last Saturday, so past simple of have

items.q: I'll get my sister ___ (help) me with my maths homework tonight.
You look different! Have you had your teeth ___ (whiten)?
Dan is at the optician's at the moment. He ___ (get) his glasses fixed.
items.why: happening now, so present continuous of get

items.q: The drama teacher got us ___ (stare) at each other without blinking.
I cut my hair at the hairdresser's every month.
a: I have my hair cut at the hairdresser's every month.
I get my hair cut at the hairdresser's every month.
items.why: someone else cuts it, so have it cut

items.q: She had painted her room by a professional.
a: She had her room painted by a professional.
items.why: the object goes before the participle

items.q: I got my brother carry the boxes.
a: I got my brother to carry the boxes.

items.q: having / we / fixed / are / tomorrow / the roof
a: We are having the roof fixed tomorrow.
Tomorrow we are having the roof fixed.

items.q: get / should / checked / you / your eyes
a: You should get your eyes checked.
Should you get your eyes checked?

units.title: Second conditional; wish and if only
notes: Form: if + past simple, would + infinitive: If I had more time, I'd learn Chinese. Never use would in the if-clause.
Use it for imaginary or unlikely situations in the present or future: If I won the lottery, I'd buy a boat. We often say If I were you.
might makes the result less certain; could means would be able to: If you asked her, she might say yes.
wish / if only + past simple for a present situation you would like to change: I wish I had a garden. wish + would for annoying habits: I wish you would listen.

items.q: If everyone ___ solar power, we would burn much less fossil fuel.
items.why: if + past simple in the second conditional

items.q: If I were you, I ___ buy a more energy efficient fridge.
We ___ reduce our carbon footprint if we cycled to school, but it isn't certain.
I wish our town ___ more renewable energy, but it doesn't.
items.why: wish + past simple for the present

items.q: If she ___ a car, she would drive us to the recycling centre.
What would you do if you ___ the president for a day?
items.why: imaginary situation, so past form after if

items.q: If only there ___ so many exhaust fumes in the city centre!
items.why: if only + past for a present situation

items.q: I ___ fly so often if trains were cheaper.
I wish people ___ stop dropping litter on the beach. It's so annoying!
If I ___ (have) more money, I'd buy an electric bike, but I'm broke.
items.why: if + past simple for an imaginary present

items.q: I'm sure the air ___ (be) cleaner if there were fewer cars, but people love driving.
items.why: would + infinitive in the result clause

items.q: If you ___ (not / waste) so much water, your bills would be lower.
What ___ (you / change) if you were the mayor of your town?
I wish I ___ (know) how to repair things instead of throwing them away.
items.why: wish + past simple for the present

items.q: Even if global warming ___ (stop) tomorrow, sea levels would still rise for years.
items.why: unlikely situation, so past simple after if

items.q: If I would have a garden, I would grow my own vegetables.
a: If I had a garden, I would grow my own vegetables.
If I had a garden, I'd grow my own vegetables.

items.q: If we recycled more, we will produce less rubbish.
a: If we recycled more, we would produce less rubbish.
If we recycled more, we'd produce less rubbish.
items.why: past simple goes with would, not will

items.q: I wish I can travel without polluting.
a: I wish I could travel without polluting.

items.q: you / where / live / would / if / you / choose / could
a: Where would you live if you could choose?
items.why: would in the question, past form after if

items.q: I'd / if / I / plant / had / more trees / a garden
a: I'd plant more trees if I had a garden.
If I had a garden, I'd plant more trees.

units.title: Modals of deduction: present
notes: must + infinitive when you are almost sure something is true: She must be tired. She's been working all day.
can't + infinitive when you are almost sure it is NOT true (never mustn't): That can't be Tom. He's in Paris.
may, might, could + infinitive when it is possible. Add well when it is quite probable: It may well rain.
For something happening now, use modal + be + -ing: They might be having dinner.

items.q: That painting is worth two million euros. The artist ___ be famous.
This ___ be a real Picasso. It only costs twenty euros!
items.why: almost sure it is not true, so can't

items.q: I have no idea who painted it. It ___ be by a local artist.
Don't go into the studio now. The artist might ___.
items.why: modal + be + -ing for an action now

items.q: He ___ not like contemporary art. Let's ask him before we buy the tickets.
The gallery is completely dark. It ___ be open today.
The exhibition has won three awards, so it may ___ be worth a visit.
items.why: may well means it is quite probable

items.q: You've been walking around the museum for six hours. You ___ be exhausted!
There's a long queue outside the gallery. The new exhibition ___ popular.
The lights are on in the studio. Someone ___ (must / be) inside.
That ___ (can't / be) the museum. It looks like a supermarket!
items.why: almost sure it is not true

items.q: Don't call her right now. She ___ (might / have) lunch with the other artists at this moment.
items.why: in progress now, so might be + -ing

items.q: I'm not certain, but this sculpture ___ (may / be) composed of recycled plastic.
He keeps looking at his watch. He ___ (must / wait) for someone.
Take a jacket. It ___ (might / not / be) warm inside the old gallery.
items.why: perhaps not, so might not + infinitive

items.q: That mustn't be the original painting. The original is in Madrid.
a: That can't be the original painting. The original is in Madrid.
That cannot be the original painting. The original is in Madrid.
That couldn't be the original painting. The original is in Madrid.
items.why: use can't, not mustn't, for deduction

items.q: She must to be very talented.
items.why: no to after a modal verb

items.q: They can be at the gallery, but I'm not sure.
a: They might be at the gallery, but I'm not sure.
They may be at the gallery, but I'm not sure.
They could be at the gallery, but I'm not sure.
items.why: use might, may or could for a present possibility

items.q: be / this painting / a lot of money / worth / must
a: This painting must be worth a lot of money.

items.q: might / in the studio / still / the artist / working / be
a: The artist might still be working in the studio.

units.title: Third conditional; wish + past perfect
notes: Form: if + past perfect, would have + past participle: If I'd seen you, I would have said hello.
Use it for imaginary situations in the past (things that did not happen) and their imagined results: If we'd left earlier, we wouldn't have missed the train.
might have means the result was only possible; could have means would have been able to: If you'd asked, I might have helped.
wish / if only + past perfect for regrets about the past: I wish I had studied more.

items.q: If she ___ harder last season, she would have got into the team.
If the firefighters had arrived later, the whole building ___.
items.why: would have + past participle for the past result

items.q: I ___ you last night if I had known you needed help.
If he hadn't shown such courage, the child ___ have survived.
items.why: a possible past result, so might not have

items.q: If you had asked me, I ___ lent you the money.
I wish I ___ round to thanking her before she left.
items.why: regret about the past, so wish + past perfect

items.q: What would you have done if you ___ your passport on that trip?
If I ___ so nervous, I could have given a better speech.
She wouldn't have got through the exam if she ___ so much determination.
If I ___ (know) about the competition last month, I would have entered it.
We ___ (not / get) lost yesterday if you had listened to me.
If they hadn't had so much team spirit, they ___ (lose) last week's final.
If only I ___ (not / say) that to her yesterday! Now she's upset.
items.why: if only + past perfect for a past regret

items.q: He ___ (get) away with it if the teacher hadn't checked his bag.
What ___ (you / do) if nobody had come to help you that night?
If I would have seen you, I would have said hello.
a: If I had seen you, I would have said hello.
If I'd seen you, I would have said hello.
If I had seen you, I'd have said hello.
If I'd seen you, I'd have said hello.

items.q: If she had had more courage, she would have tell the truth.
a: If she had had more courage, she would have told the truth.

items.q: I wish I didn't shout at my brother last night.
a: I wish I hadn't shouted at my brother last night.
I wish I had not shouted at my brother last night.
items.why: a past regret needs the past perfect

items.q: had / if / it / rained / we / cancelled / would have / the race
a: If it had rained, we would have cancelled the race.
We would have cancelled the race if it had rained.
items.why: if + past perfect, would have + participle

items.q: wish / I / I / had / advice / listened to / your
a: I wish I had listened to your advice.

units.title: Modals of deduction: past
notes: Use modal + have + past participle to make guesses about the past.
must have when you are almost sure it happened: The grass is wet. It must have rained.
can't have / couldn't have when you are almost sure it didn't happen: She can't have left. Her coat is still here.
may have, might have, could have when perhaps it happened: He might have missed the bus.

items.q: The window is broken and the TV has gone. A burglar ___ in.
The suspect ___ the theft. He was in hospital that night.
I don't know how the hacker got my password. I ___ it on a fake website.
She got the top mark in the law exam. She must have ___ really hard.
The police think the prisoner ___ escaped through the basement.
The jury ___ have believed the witness, because they found the man guilty.
items.why: a logical conclusion about the past

items.q: Nobody saw the burglars. They ___ in through the back door.
He ___ the money. He's the most honest person I know.
Where's my wallet? I ___ it in the shop, or perhaps it's in the car.
The door wasn't forced. The thief ___ (must / have) a key.
She ___ (can't / forget) the meeting. I reminded her an hour ago.
I can't find my keys. I ___ (might / drop) them on the bus this morning.
The judge released him, so the police ___ (must / make) a mistake.
items.why: a logical conclusion about the past

items.q: They ___ (may / not / receive) my statement yet. I only sent it this morning.
Look, footprints! Someone ___ (must / walk) across the garden last night.
items.why: evidence now about a past action

items.q: He must have went home early.
a: He must have gone home early.

items.q: She mustn't have heard the alarm, because she didn't wake up.
a: She can't have heard the alarm, because she didn't wake up.
She couldn't have heard the alarm, because she didn't wake up.
She cannot have heard the alarm, because she didn't wake up.
items.why: use can't have for negative deduction

items.q: The thief might has escaped by car.
a: The thief might have escaped by car.

items.q: have / the hacker / must / my password / guessed
a: The hacker must have guessed my password.

items.q: can't / the victim / the burglar / have / clearly / seen
a: The victim can't have seen the burglar clearly.
The burglar can't have seen the victim clearly.
The victim can't have clearly seen the burglar.
The burglar can't have clearly seen the victim.

units.title: -ing forms
notes: The -ing form can be the subject or object of a sentence: Swimming is great exercise. I've finished tidying my room.
Use -ing after verbs of liking and disliking (love, enjoy, hate, can't stand, don't mind): I can't stand queuing.
Always use -ing after a preposition: She's good at drawing. He left without saying goodbye. I'm looking forward to seeing you.
An -ing clause can give a reason or describe what someone is doing: Feeling hungry, we stopped for a sandwich. I saw a man climbing a wall.

items.q: ___ a shed is more time-consuming than it looks.
I can't stand ___ in the cold basement.
She's very good at ___ old furniture.
He climbed the ladder without ___ if it was safe.
I'm tired of ___ for the bus on that uncomfortable bench.
When we walked past, we saw two men ___ the chimney.
items.why: see + person + -ing for an action in progress

items.q: ___ tired after the climb, we rested in a mountain hut.
Do you mind ___ me to carry this rug upstairs?
Thank you for ___ us use the community centre.
My dad has just finished ___ (paint) the garden shed.
In my opinion, ___ (live) in a concrete tower block is depressing.
Are you interested in ___ (join) the project at the community centre?
Not ___ (want) to wake anyone, she walked quietly down the steps.
They enjoy ___ (sit) on the bench outside the shelter in the evening.
She left the building without ___ (lock) the door.
I'm looking forward to see your new house.
a: I'm looking forward to seeing your new house.
I am looking forward to seeing your new house.
items.why: to is a preposition here, so -ing

items.q: Swim in the sea is great exercise.
a: Swimming in the sea is great exercise.

items.q: He is afraid of to climb the ladder.
a: He is afraid of climbing the ladder.
He's afraid of climbing the ladder.

items.q: is / without / a ladder / dangerous / the roof / climbing onto
a: Climbing onto the roof without a ladder is dangerous.

items.q: mind / I / sleeping / in the basement / don't
a: I don't mind sleeping in the basement.
